Second half, prove nothing changed: one date typed into the attestation field turned 'no regulatory limit has ever been changed in this system' into 'no regulatory limit has changed from 2026-01-01 onward, checked on 2026-08-07' in 1,512 ms. Total 1,625 ms against targets of 15 s and 30 s and a baseline that called the second half unbuildable. JS-13 (revenue owner changes a price): 3 clicks, rate card ready 135 ms after leaving the landing screen, money delta on screen 688 ms after the edit blurred and before any save: 142.2122 -> 156.4334 ILS per second and 40,803,530 -> 44,883,883 ILS with 4,080,353 named as 10 percent of the plan, both scoped to the operator's own channel over 2,540 planned segments, with 'save the rate card' and 'discard the edit' both offered. Total 4,916 ms against a 45 s target and a baseline of no delta at all. I did not save, to avoid writing the shared settings store. JS-4 (programming representative registers a restriction): 3,188 ms from first keystroke to the rule saved and read back, 8 acts, against a 30 s target and a baseline of cannot start. The preview named the five breaks that would go with their dates, times and lengths, priced them at -66,024 ILS (10,147,561 -> 10,081,538) over the operator's own channel and 7 broadcast days, and refused the second basis honestly rather than guessing it. Zero engine words on the path (checked fix_offset, offset_seconds, predicate, regex, pin_count, where_json, constraint_id: none rendered). The saved rule reads back as a Hebrew sentence with who asked, why and when it stopped applying. Nothing is slower than the baseline and every target is met with two orders of magnitude of headroom.
bars.bar_2_reference: Both references reached as documentation; neither dashboard is reachable without an account and I did not invent what I could not see. Linear (linear.app/docs/sla, fetched live): rules are written and displayed as one plain sentence with a trigger and an effect, 'When Priority is Urgent, add a 24 hour SLA', and the docs describe no creator, no reason and no expiry on the rule. Meridian's own restriction register is the same sentence register and carries three things Linear's does not: 'asked by <person>', the reason, and the date it stopped applying. Meridian wins that comparison, on the surface that matters for JS-4. Where it loses is the second register on the same screen: the condition builder lists all 7 rows of the same rule in English to a Hebrew reader, which Linear never does. Stripe: dashboard.stripe.com is behind a login, so I read docs.stripe.com/radar/rules for the mechanic instead and say so plainly. Stripe's pre-save statement is a dedicated step: Test rule, then a 'Review new rule' page that simulates the last 6 months of charges and reports how many legitimate, fraudulent and blocked payments the rule would have hit, filterable by payment method, and only then 'Add rule'. Meridian's is stronger on naming and honesty and weaker on coverage: it names the individual breaks the rule removes rather than a count, prices them in money, states the scope the figures were taken over, and when the exact re-run basis is too expensive it says so and tells the person how to narrow rather than printing an estimate; but at the default scope of 7 broadcast days that second basis is refused, so the operator confirms on the counted basis, where Stripe would have simulated. Net: Meridian is ahead on the effect-before-save mechanic and ahead of Linear on how a rule reads, except where the rule is read back in the wrong language.
